NEW YORK (CNN) -- Five new cases of the H1N1 virus in New York City schools will force three schools to close for a week, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said at a news conference Thursday evening. The city is temporarily closing the schools to "slow transmission" of the virus, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said. The two intermediate schools and one primary school are in Queens, and all three will be closed for at least five days, the mayor said. "We are closing the schools to slow transmission" of sickness, he said. Bloomberg, flanked by New York Gov. David Paterson and New York City School Chancellor Joel Klein, said four students at one of the intermediate schools have the virus and an administrator was critically ill Thursday with H1N1. Bloomberg indicated the school administrator had a pre-existing medical condition. Fifty students at that school have been sent home with flu-like symptoms since May 6. At the two other schools, the primary school had an overflowing nurse's office Thursday, reporting 29 students suffering from flu-like symptoms. The other intermediate school had 241 students absent with illness Thursday. The New York City Department of Health and the Department of Education have been in nearly constant contact, said Jason Post, a spokesman from Bloomberg's office. When there's a spike in students absent from classes, the Department of Health is alerted. "There's always good communication, flu or no flu," Post said. "But our senses have been sharp for a while now." The Health Department has seen a general increase in flu activity in Queens, officials said in a news release. While the symptoms of H1N1 flu seem to resemble those of seasonal flu, the H1N1 virus appears to spread more extensively, at least in schools, warranting closures to slow transmission in the community, the release said. Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, the deputy commissioner of the city's Department of Hygiene and Mental Health, said although concern is legitimate, there's no solid evidence that suggests the H1N1 flu -- also known as swine flu -- is more dangerous than the flu in general. "The bottom line is if you're sick, stay home," Weisfuse said. "And don't go back to school until you're better for one whole day." In late April, St. Francis Prep, a high school in Queens, was closed because of a flu outbreak. Since then, the school reopened and the stricken students have recovered, according to the mayor's office. "As we have said from the outset of the appearance of H1N1 in our city last month, we will share with New Yorkers what we know and not speculate on what we don't know," said Bloomberg in a statement. According to the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as of Thursday night 7,412 cases of H1N1 flu have been confirmed worldwide. The organizations said 63 deaths attributed to the virus have been confirmed worldwide. The CDC said 4,298 cases of the virus and three fatalities have been confirmed in the United States as of Thursday night. New York had 224 confirmed cases of H1N1, the CDC said. It was not clear whether the five cases cited by Bloomberg and the other New York officials were included in the latest CDC total.

Flanked by New York Gov. The affected institutions—two intermediate schools and a primary school, all located in Queens—will remain shuttered for a minimum of five days. "We are closing the schools to slow transmission" of the illness, the mayor explained during his announcement.

Standing alongside Governor David Paterson and Schools Chancellor Joel Klein, Bloomberg revealed that four pupils at one intermediate school had tested positive for the virus, while a school administrator remained in critical condition due to H1N1. The mayor noted this administrator had suffered from an underlying health issue beforehand. Since May 6, roughly fifty students from that same institution had been dismissed due to flu-like symptoms.

Conditions at the other two schools proved similarly concerning. The primary school's nursing station was overwhelmed Thursday, handling 29 cases of students displaying influenza symptoms. Meanwhile, the second intermediate school recorded 241 sick-related absences that same day.

Jason Post, speaking on behalf of the mayor's office, explained that health and education officials had maintained constant coordination throughout the situation. Any noticeable uptick in student absences triggers immediate notification to health authorities. "There's always good communication, flu or no flu," Post remarked, "but our senses have been sharp for a while now."

City health officials confirmed a broader surge in flu-related activity across Queens. Their statement noted that although H1N1 symptoms closely mirror those of ordinary seasonal influenza, the virus seems to transmit more aggressively—particularly within school environments—justifying the decision to temporarily close facilities as a preventive measure.

Dr. Isaac Weisfuse, deputy health commissioner, acknowledged public anxiety was understandable but stressed that no conclusive evidence indicates H1N1 poses greater danger than typical flu strains. His advice was straightforward: "The bottom line is if you're sick, stay home. And don't go back to school until you're better for one whole day."

This isn't the city's first brush with flu-related school closures—St. Francis Prep, a Queens high school, had shut down in late April amid a similar outbreak. That institution has since reopened, with affected students having fully recovered, per information from the mayor's office.

"As we have said from the outset of the appearance of H1N1 in our city last month, we will share with New Yorkers what we know and not speculate on what we don't know," Bloomberg stated.

Global figures released by the World Health Organization and the CDC showed 7,412 confirmed H1N1 cases worldwide as of Thursday night, with 63 deaths linked to the virus internationally. Within the United States, the CDC reported 4,298 confirmed infections and three fatalities. New York State alone accounted for 224 verified cases, according to CDC data. Whether the five new cases announced by city officials had already been factored into these federal totals remained unclear.

New York City health officials announced today the temporary closure of three public schools in Queens for a minimum of five days after five new cases of the H1N1 virus, commonly known as swine flu, were confirmed among students. The decision comes as part of an increasingly cautious approach by city officials to prevent further spread of the virus within school communities.

According to representatives from the city's Health Department, the affected schools reported unusual spikes in student absenteeism over the past week, with a notable increase in reports of flu-like symptoms including fever, cough, and sore throat. Unlike seasonal flu, which tends to disproportionately affect the elderly and very young children, H1N1 has shown a tendency to affect school-age children and young adults at higher rates, prompting additional scrutiny of educational institutions as potential outbreak sites.

Health officials have reiterated their commitment to closely monitoring the situation across the city's five boroughs, noting that additional school closures may be necessary if similar patterns of illness and absenteeism are detected elsewhere. **NYC Closes Three Schools as H1N1 Cases Rise**

*By CNN Staff*

NEW YORK (CNN) — New York City health officials announced Wednesday that three public schools would be temporarily closed after a cluster of H1N1 swine flu cases was confirmed among students, marking one of the most significant school closures in the city since the virus first emerged.

The affected schools, located in Queens and the Bronx, will remain closed for at least seven days as a precautionary measure, according to the city's Department of Education and the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene. Officials said dozens of students at the schools reported flu-like symptoms in recent days, prompting health workers to conduct rapid testing that confirmed several cases of the H1N1 strain.

"We are taking this seriously, but I want to stress that we are not panicking," Mayor Michael Bloomberg said at a press conference held outside City Hall. "The vast majority of children who contract this virus experience mild symptoms and recover quickly. Closing these schools is a precautionary step to prevent further spread, not an indication that we are facing a citywide crisis."

Bloomberg, joined by Health Commissioner Dr. Thomas Farley, emphasized that the decision to close the schools was made in consultation with federal health officials and was consistent with guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

"We're following the science here," Bloomberg said. "When you see a concentration of cases in a school setting, the responsible thing to do is to interrupt that chain of transmission. That means closing the doors for a short period, cleaning the facilities thoroughly, and monitoring the situation closely."

City health officials said parents of students at the affected schools have been notified and encouraged to keep their children home, monitor them for fever, cough, and sore throat, and contact a physician if symptoms worsen. Free flu testing sites have also been set up in the affected neighborhoods.

Bloomberg sought to reassure parents across the five boroughs that the city was prepared for a broader outbreak if one were to occur.

"We have contingency plans in place. We have stockpiles of antiviral medication, and we are working closely with hospitals to ensure they have the resources they need," he said. "I want every parent in this city to know that we are watching this situation minute by minute."

The mayor also urged New Yorkers to practice basic preventive measures — frequent handwashing, staying home when sick, and covering coughs and sneezes — calling them "the single most effective tools we have" against the virus's spread.

Some parents outside the closed schools expressed a mix of concern and relief Wednesday morning.

"I'm glad they're being cautious," said Maria Delgado, whose daughter attends one of the closed schools. "But it's also scary. You don't want your kid to be one of the ones who gets sick."

City officials said they would reassess the situation at the end of the week and determine whether additional precautions, including further school closures, would be necessary. The Department of Education said make-up days would be scheduled later in the academic year to ensure students do not fall behind.

Bloomberg closed his remarks by striking a note of calm.

"New Yorkers have faced challenges before, and we've always gotten through them by working together and staying informed," he said. "This is no different. We will get through this flu season, and we will do it responsibly."

Health officials nationwide have been monitoring H1N1 activity closely since the virus first drew global attention, with schools frequently serving as early indicators of localized outbreaks due to close contact among students.

The CDC has not yet commented specifically on the New York closures but reiterated that school districts have the authority to make closure decisions based on local conditions.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*

# City Schools Close as H1N1 Cases Mount, Bloomberg Announces

**NEW YORK** — Mayor Michael Bloomberg announced Wednesday that several New York City public schools would close temporarily following a spike in confirmed and suspected cases of H1N1 influenza, marking one of the most significant public health responses the city has undertaken since the virus first emerged.

Standing before a bank of television cameras at City Hall, flanked by Health Commissioner Dr. Thomas Farley and Schools Chancellor officials, Bloomberg struck a measured but urgent tone.

"We are taking this step out of an abundance of caution," Bloomberg said. "Our first obligation is to protect the health of our children, our teachers, and our school communities, while making sure the city continues to function."

## The Numbers

According to figures released by the Health Department, the city has recorded a cluster of confirmed H1N1 cases concentrated in a handful of schools across Queens and the Bronx, with health officials citing "several hundred" students exhibiting flu-like symptoms over the preceding week. Dr. Farley told reporters that of those tested, a significant majority returned presumptive positive results for the H1N1 strain, though he cautioned that testing capacity limitations meant the true number of cases was likely higher.

"We are seeing absentee rates in some schools climb well above what we'd consider typical for this time of year," Farley said. "When we see that kind of clustering, combined with confirmed positive tests, it tells us transmission is happening within these school communities, and that warrants action."

Citywide, health officials estimated symptomatic absenteeism had risen sharply in affected districts, prompting the decision to close roughly a dozen schools for an initial period, with the possibility of extending closures depending on how the situation develops.

## Health Department Guidance

Dr. Farley emphasized that the closures were a precautionary measure rather than a sign of uncontrolled outbreak, noting that H1N1 symptoms in most confirmed cases had been mild.

"The vast majority of people who contract this virus recover fully without hospitalization," he said. "But we know certain populations — young children, pregnant women, and people with underlying conditions — face higher risks, and schools are, by their nature, environments where respiratory viruses spread efficiently."

He urged parents to keep symptomatic children home regardless of whether their school was among those closed, and reiterated standard guidance: frequent handwashing, covering coughs, and seeking medical attention if symptoms worsened, particularly difficulty breathing or persistent high fever.

Farley also addressed vaccine availability, telling reporters the city was coordinating with federal health authorities to expedite distribution once supply increased, though he acknowledged initial shipments would be limited and prioritized for high-risk groups.

## Mayor's Remarks on Continuity

Bloomberg sought to reassure families that closures were localized and temporary, pushing back on suggestions that a broader, citywide shutdown of schools was imminent.

"This is not a decision to close the entire school system," he said. "We are following the data, school by school, and acting where the evidence tells us we need to act. If conditions change, our response will change with it."

He added that the city was coordinating meal programs and childcare guidance for affected families, acknowledging the disruption closures cause for working parents.

"We understand this creates real hardship," Bloomberg said. "We're working to minimize that burden while keeping kids safe."

## Looking Ahead

Officials said affected schools would undergo cleaning protocols before reopening and that attendance and symptom data would be closely monitored in surrounding districts. Farley indicated the Health Department would issue updated case counts as more test results became available, and did not rule out additional closures if absentee rates continued to climb elsewhere in the city.

The press conference concluded with Bloomberg fielding questions on vaccine timelines and school reopening criteria, though officials offered no firm date for when closed schools would resume classes, stating only that the decision would be "guided by the science and the data as they develop."

*This is a developing story.*
